newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 11.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for Reuters by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Hindustan Times
CONGRESS CHIEF PREPARES FOR ATTACK

The Congress leadership faced fresh opposition from within following the party's defeat in the Punjab assembly polls. It, however, braced itself to answer critics by attributing the verdict to the people's desire for change and the party's neglect of organisational matters in the last five years. Although the defeat was expected, the extent of damage did surprise and shock party chief Sitaram Kesri and his aides. Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's supporters, however, demanded a discussion of Kesri's actions, who in their view was responsible for the party's debacle.
The Times Of India
ATOMIC ENERGY ACT MAY BE AMENDED

The government is considering amending atomic energy norms to allow the participation of private firms in promoting and generating nuclear power. The amendment seemed unavoidable after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda publicly invited 100 percent foreign-owned nuclear power plants in the country, government sources said. Presently, only the government could produce, develop, use and dispose off atomic energy and carry out research into matters connected with it. Of late, some countries have shown an interest in the nuclear power sector, despite India's not being a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The Economic Times
CELLULAR OPERATORS TAKE DOT TO COURT

The process of telecommunications privatisation took another blow with cellular operators taking the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) to court. This stemmed from DoT's recent decision to start charging fixed line subscribers a maximum of 10 rupees per minute to call a cellular phone from February 15, 1997. This was regardless of the fact whether the mobile phone called was in the same city or the same circle. About 50 percent of all calls for cellular phones originated from DoT's fixed line network, industry sources said. With the new tariffs in place, such calls were expected to decline to five percent of total calls.
PRIVATE AIRLINES TO GET ONE YEAR TO INCREASE FLEET

The Civil Aviation Ministry may give a year's time to private operators to meet the minimum fleet size requirement of five aircraft and a higher minimum equity, as mandated by the civil aviation policy announced recently. The policy also laid down that a minimum 50 million rupee equity be maintained by firms operating small aircraft and a minimum 300 million equity by those operating big aircraft. The idea of a minimum fleet was to strengthen domestic airlines and make them viable to take on social obligations such as flying uneconomic routes.
TAX BREAKS FOR OIL EXPLORATION

The Petroleum Ministry proposes offering tax holidays to firms investing in high-risk exploration blocks. Sources said the ministry also mooted setting up of a band which would restrict the total tax burden between 10 and 20 percent on high-risk oil exploration. This proposal, which has got a favourable response from the Finance Ministry, will be put up for cabinet approval as a part of the new exploration licensing policy.
Financial Express
RUSH FOR FRESH SUGAR LICENCES DESPITE GLUT

Investors are seeking fresh sugar licences despite the projected glut in the industry. Private players in the sugar industry have swung into action with the government opening a floodgate of licensing much beyond the existing sugarcane availability. Ever since assuming Office, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government has been on a sugar licensing binge, issuing a record number of 95 licences until November 1996. The sugar manufacturers' associations have been complaining of a steep fall in the sugarcane availability this season because of low production and shift in crop pattern from sugarcane to wheat.
CABINET DISCUSSION ON CIVIL AVIATION POLICY DEFERRED

Hectic political and corporate lobbying forced Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to put off the finalisation of foreign investment norms for private airlines and airports in the country. Sources said the prime minister may refer the civil aviation policy issue to the coalition government's steering committee, which was scheduled to meet on February 18, 1997. This was an attempt to work out a compromise decision, given the controversy the policy has generated. The prime minister hoped a political consensus could be worked out at the committee meeting on allowing the Tata-Singapore Airlines proposal to go through, albeit in a modified format.
ESSAR OIL QUITS OFFSHORE DRILLING SELLS TWO RIGS

Essar Oil, which was in the midst of implementing its nine million-tonne oil refinery project, sold off its two offshore oil rigs for 1.9 billion rupees. At least one rig has been sold to the Noble Drilling (USA)/Neddrill (Netherlands) group, sources said. These rigs, presently charter-hired to the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation, were expected to be delivered to the buyers by April 1997. The company said it decided to shift its focus from offshore drilling to onshore drilling activity in view of global trends in the business.
Business Standard
EXIM POLICY RELIEF FOR FARM, MARINE PRODUCTS PROPOSED

The Commerce Ministry may introduce a major package for exporters of agricultural and marine products in the forthcoming Export-Import (Exim) policy for April 1997/2002. The incentives were expected to be mentioned in a fresh chapter, which would be incorporated in the new policy. The current Exim policy does not have a chapter on agricultural products. The Commerce Ministry also planned to take up the issue of granting industry status to cash crops with the Agriculture Ministry.
FISCAL DEFICIT TO BE CAPPED AT 4.5 PCT NEXT YEAR

The fiscal deficit target for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year was expected to be pegged between four and 4.5 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP), government sources said. This was in keeping with the ruling coalition's common minimum programme that sought to progressively pare fiscal deficit to a level of four percent of GDP. The government was likely to end the current financial year with a fiscal deficit of around 5.2 percent compared with the target of five percent.
The Observer
SOPS FOR NON-DOMESTIC SATELLITE TV SERVICES

Non-domestic satellite TV, restricted local TV/radio broadcast services of non-commercial nature and other such services, as may be notified by the government, would be exempted from the bidding process for the grant of licences. This was proposed by the Information and Broadcasting Ministry.
REGULATOR EXPLORING OPTIONS TO AVOID DELISTING

The stock market regulator (SEBI) initiated an exercise to find out alternatives to delisting of companies by stock exchanges for flouting the norms of the bourses. The move comes in the wake of the Bombay bourse's decision to consider the delisting of 190 companies, which failed to pay the listing fees for fiscal 1996/97. The issue of investors suffering due to delisting of firms came up at the last meeting of the inter-exchange coordination group.
CEMENT OUTPUT LIKELY TO BE HIT

Cement production in 1996/97 (April-March) was likely to be affected adversely by the increase in oil prices due to high transport intensity of the industry. A central bank study on industrial production said installed capacity was targeted to grow by 7.9 percent against the targeted growth rate of 9.2 percent during 1996/97. The projected growth in demand was lower at 2.8 percent in 1996/97.
